lessons.title: Lesson 26: ~는 것 Describing Nouns with Verbs

vocab.en: to recognize, to try to know
to smoke, to light a fire of some sort
to be remaining, to be left over

grammar.explanation:
~는 lets a verb describe a noun, the way ~ㄴ/은 does for adjectives. The verb and everything in front of it form one describing clause, and the noun comes last: 뛰는 학생 is "a student who runs / is running". Use it for actions happening now or in general.

To form it, add ~는 to the stem. A final consonant makes no difference: 가다 → 가 + 는 → 가는, 먹다 → 먹 + 는 → 먹는. The one change is with ㄹ-stems, which lose the ㄹ: 살다 → 사 + 는 → 사는, 팔다 → 파는.

Build the clause in normal Korean order and move the noun to the end. 학생이 복도에서 뛰어요 (the student runs in the hallway) becomes 복도에서 뛰는 학생 (the student running in the hallway). The noun's old particle disappears; the new particle goes after the noun.

Don't mix this up with adjectives: adjectives use ~ㄴ/은 for the present (예쁜, 작은), but verbs use ~는. On a verb, ~ㄴ/은 means past: 먹은 사람 is "the person who ate", not "who eats".

examples.en: I saw a student running in the hallway.
There are many people who smoke.
The older woman who lives in our neighborhood is kind.
The person singing over there is my older brother.
The kimchi that woman sells is delicious.
examples.note: 팔다 is an ㄹ-stem, so the ㄹ drops: 팔 + 는 → 파는.

examples.en: What is the song you're listening to now?
examples.note: ~는 starts with a consonant, so the ㄷ irregular doesn't apply: 듣다 → 듣는.

grammar.explanation:
For an action that is already finished, a verb takes ~ㄴ/은 to describe a noun: 산 물건 is "the item (someone) bought". The whole phrase works as one noun, so it can take any particle.

After a vowel, put ㄴ under the last syllable: 사다 → 사 + ㄴ → 산, 만나다 → 만난, 하다 → 한. After a consonant, add ~은: 먹다 → 먹 + 은 → 먹은, 읽다 → 읽은. ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ and take ㄴ: 만들다 → 만든.

This looks just like the adjective modifier (예쁜, 작은), but on a verb it means past. 먹은 음식 is "food I ate"; "food I am eating" is 먹는 음식. Don't add ~았/었 as well: it is 산 물건, never 샀은 물건.

examples.ko: 제가 어제 산 물건이 너무 비싸요.
examples.en: The item I bought yesterday is too expensive.
The player who got hurt in the game is in the hospital.
The student who passed the exam is my friend.
The bread I ate this morning was tasty.
Who is the person who wrote this letter?
The cake my younger sibling made is too sweet.
examples.note: 만들다 drops its ㄹ: 만들 + ㄴ → 만든.

grammar.explanation:
~ㄹ/을 describes a noun with an action that hasn't happened yet: 먹을 음식 is "food (I) will eat" or "food to eat". It often matches English "to do" phrases, like 할 일 (things to do) or 입을 옷 (clothes to wear).

After a vowel, put ㄹ under the last syllable: 가다 → 가 + ㄹ → 갈, 보다 → 볼, 하다 → 할. After a consonant, add ~을: 먹다 → 먹 + 을 → 먹을, 읽다 → 읽을. A stem that already ends in ㄹ stays as it is: 살다 → 살, 만들다 → 만들.

This is the same piece inside ~ㄹ/을 거예요 (것이다): 먹을 거예요 is literally "it is a thing (I) will eat". So the three verb modifiers line up by time: 먹은 (ate), 먹는 (eat / am eating), 먹을 (will eat).

examples.en: I bought food to eat tomorrow.
The destination I will go to is Busan.
There is a game I will watch this weekend.
I have a lot of things to do this weekend.
I don't have any clothes to wear to the party.

examples.ko: 우리가 살 집은 학교 근처에 있어요.
examples.en: The house we will live in is near the school.
examples.note: 살다 already ends in ㄹ, so the future form is just 살.

grammar.point: ~는 것 (turning an action into a noun)
grammar.explanation:
When the noun after a describing clause is 것 ("thing"), the clause becomes a noun: 걷는 것 is "walking" or "the act of walking". This lets you use a whole action as the subject or object: "Walking is dangerous", "I hate smoking".

Build it like any other described noun: stem + ~는 + 것. 공부하다 → 공부하는 것, 먹다 → 먹는 것, 만들다 → 만드는 것. Then add the particle you need: 것은 / 것이 for the subject, 것을 for the object. In speech these shrink: 것은 → 건, 것이 → 게, 것을 → 걸.

The tense of the modifier changes the meaning. ~는 것 is the action in general ("eating"). With the past ~ㄴ/은 것, it is the specific thing someone did: 말한 것 is "what (he) said". With the future ~ㄹ/을 것 it is something to do: 먹을 것 is "something to eat".

examples.en: Walking alone at night is dangerous.
I hate smoking.
Studying Korean is fun.
Do you believe what that person said?
My hobby is taking photos.
Resting at home is the best.
examples.note: 게 is the spoken short form of 것이.

examples.en: There's nothing to eat in the fridge.

lessons.title: Lesson 27: Using ~던/었던 to Describe Past Tense

vocab.en: to transfer on a bus, subway

grammar.explanation:
~던 describes a noun with an action the speaker remembers from the past: 자주 가던 약국 is "the pharmacy I used to go to often". It looks back at a past habit, or at an action that was in progress and wasn't finished (it may even still be going on).

Forming it is easy: add ~던 straight to any stem. Vowels, consonants and ㄹ-stems make no difference: 가다 → 가 + 던 → 가던, 먹다 → 먹 + 던 → 먹던, 살다 → 살던.

Compare it with the past modifier ~ㄴ/은. 먹은 햄버거 is a hamburger that was eaten, finished. 먹던 햄버거 is one someone was eating and didn't finish, so some of it is probably still there. With repeated actions, ~던 adds the feel of "used to": 제가 다니던 학교 is "the school I used to go to".

Because it suits ongoing or repeated actions, ~던 sounds odd with one-time events such as being born.

examples.ko: 제가 자주 가던 약국이 문을 닫았어요.
examples.en: The pharmacy I used to go to often closed down.
This is the notebook I used every day.

examples.ko: 형이 입던 옷을 지금 제가 입어요.
examples.en: I now wear the clothes my older brother used to wear.

examples.ko: 손님이 먹던 햄버거가 아직 테이블에 있어요.
examples.en: The hamburger the guest was eating is still on the table.

examples.ko: 제가 살던 집은 바다 근처에 있었어요.
examples.en: The house I used to live in was near the sea.
examples.note: ~던 never changes the stem: 살다 → 살던.

examples.en: Where is the book I was reading earlier?

examples.ko: 할머니가 쓰던 숟가락을 아직 가지고 있어요.
examples.en: I still have the spoon my grandmother used to use.

grammar.explanation:
~았/었던 also describes a noun with a past action, but it stresses that the action is completely over. 갔던 곳 is "the place I went to (back then)", a finished experience you are recalling.

To form it, take the past polite form, drop 어요 and add 던: 가다 → 갔어요 → 갔던, 먹다 → 먹었어요 → 먹었던, 하다 → 했어요 → 했던, 보다 → 봤어요 → 봤던. Irregulars follow the past tense as usual: 듣다 → 들었던, 돕다 → 도왔던.

How it differs: 먹던 음식 is food someone was eating (maybe unfinished, maybe a habit). 먹었던 음식 is food that was eaten and is done, remembered from the past. Often the plain past modifier works too (먹은 음식); ~았/었던 just adds a stronger "back then, and it's over" feeling.

examples.en: The embassy I went to last year was very big.
The movie I saw yesterday had interesting content.
Now I know the reason I failed.
I met a nurse who had worked in Korea.
The company I used to work at was far from home.

examples.ko: 그때 들었던 노래를 다시 듣고 싶어요.
examples.en: I want to listen again to the song I heard back then.
examples.note: 듣다 → 들었어요, so the form is 들었던.

examples.en: Do you remember the café where we first met?

grammar.explanation:
Adjectives can take ~았/었던 to describe a noun by a state that was true before but isn't anymore: 작았던 동생 is "my sibling who used to be small".

Form it the same way as with verbs: past polite form, drop 어요, add 던. 작다 → 작았어요 → 작았던, 외롭다 → 외로웠어요 → 외로웠던, 바쁘다 → 바빴어요 → 바빴던, 조용하다 → 조용했어요 → 조용했던.

Compare it with the present adjective modifier ~ㄴ/은. 작은 동생 says how the sibling is now. 작았던 동생 points back to how they were, and suggests it has changed.

examples.en: The lonely times have all passed.

examples.ko: 어렸을 때 작았던 동생이 이제 키가 커요.
examples.en: My younger sibling, who was small as a kid, is tall now.

examples.ko: 소중했던 기억을 영원히 잊지 않을 거예요.
examples.en: I will never forget those precious memories.
The neighborhood that used to be quiet is very noisy now.
The busy week is finally over.
examples.note: 바쁘다 drops ㅡ: 바쁘 + 았 → 바빴.

examples.en: The weather, which was cold, has gotten a lot warmer.

vocab.en: to stand something up, to line something up
to be enough, to be sufficient
to be familiar with, to be close with

grammar.explanation:
Verb modifiers meet the irregular rules from Lesson 7. What matters is how the ending starts. ~는 starts with a consonant, so only ㄹ-stems change: the ㄹ drops (만들다 → 만드는, 살다 → 사는). ㄷ, ㅂ and ㅅ stems stay as they are: 듣는, 돕는, 짓는.

~은 and ~을 start with a vowel sound, so they trigger the vowel irregulars. ㄷ becomes ㄹ: 걷다 → 걸 + 은 → 걸은, 듣다 → 들을. ㅂ becomes 우: 돕다 → 도우 + ㄴ → 도운, 춥다 → 추운. ㅅ drops: 짓다 → 지 + 은 → 지은.

ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ before ㄴ (만들다 → 만든, 팔다 → 판) and keep it for the future, adding nothing (만들다 → 만들, 살다 → 살). A common mistake is 만들은 or 만들을: there is never an extra 으 after an ㄹ-stem.

examples.en: The food my mom makes is the most delicious.
The road I walked yesterday was very long.
I greeted the person who helped me.
The story I heard is true.

examples.ko: 이 집은 제 할아버지가 지은 집이에요.
examples.en: This house is one my grandfather built.
examples.note: 짓다 drops ㅅ before 은: 지 + 은 → 지은.

examples.ko: 내일 들을 수업은 아침 아홉 시에 있어요.
examples.en: The class I'll take tomorrow is at nine in the morning.
examples.note: 듣다: ㄷ becomes ㄹ before 을, so 들을.

examples.ko: 추운 날에는 따뜻한 차를 마시고 싶어요.
examples.en: On cold days I want to drink hot tea.

grammar.explanation:
Korean has no word for "favorite". Instead you describe the noun as "the one I like most": 제가 + 제일/가장 + 좋아하는 + noun. 제가 제일 좋아하는 음식 is literally "the food that I like most", which means "my favorite food".

Step by step: start with the sentence 제가 음식을 제일 좋아해요. Turn 좋아해요 into the modifier 좋아하는 and move the noun to the end: 제가 제일 좋아하는 음식. Then use it as the topic: 제가 제일 좋아하는 음식은 김치예요.

Use 제가/내가 (subject), not 저의/나의, because "I" is the one doing the liking. For someone else, swap in their name or 네가: 네가 가장 좋아하는 계절. If your favorite is an activity, turn that into a noun with ~는 것 too: 제가 제일 좋아하는 것은 노래하는 것이에요. 가장 and 제일 mean the same; 제일 is a little more casual.

examples.en: My favorite sport is basketball.

examples.ko: 제가 제일 좋아하는 것은 친구와 배구를 하는 것이에요.
examples.en: My favorite thing is playing volleyball with friends.
What is your favorite season?
My favorite food is kimchi stew.

examples.ko: 민수 씨가 가장 좋아하는 가수는 누구예요?
examples.en: Who is Minsu's favorite singer?

examples.ko: 제가 제일 좋아했던 선생님은 수학 선생님이었어요.
examples.en: My favorite teacher was my math teacher.
examples.note: 좋아했던 talks about a favorite from the past.

grammar.point: Describing nouns with 싶다, 있다 and 없다
grammar.explanation:
Three common words take a modifier you might not expect. 싶다 is an adjective, so it uses the adjective form ~ㄴ/은: 가고 싶다 → 가고 싶 + 은 → 가고 싶은. 가고 싶은 곳 is "a place I want to go".

있다 and 없다 work the other way. Even though 재미있다 and 맛없다 feel like adjectives, they take ~는, like verbs: 재미있다 → 재미있 + 는 → 재미있는, 맛있다 → 맛있는, 돈이 없다 → 돈이 없는. So it is 재미있는 영화, never 재미있은 영화.

For the past, both use ~았/었던: 재미있었던 영화 (a movie that was fun), 가고 싶었던 곳 (a place I had wanted to go).

examples.en: The country I want to go to is Canada.
Yesterday I saw a funny advertisement.

examples.ko: 돈이 없는 사람도 이 농장에서 일할 수 있어요.
examples.en: Even people with no money can work on this farm.

examples.ko: 시간이 없는 날에는 집에서 밥을 먹어요.
examples.en: On days I have no time, I eat at home.
What I want to eat is tteokbokki.

examples.ko: 정말 가고 싶었던 공연을 드디어 봤어요.
examples.en: I finally saw the performance I really wanted to go to.

grammar.point: Where 그/이/저/나의 go in modified nouns
grammar.explanation:
Words like 이, 그, 저 (this, that) and 나의 / 저의 / 제 (my) belong to the noun itself, so they sit right in front of it. When a noun also has a describing clause, the clause comes first and the small word comes last, just before the noun.

Build it in two steps. Start with the noun and its small word: 그 사람. Then put the describing clause in front of the whole thing: 내가 만난 + 그 사람 → 내가 만난 그 사람 (that person I met). Possessives work the same way: 어제 산 + 제 가방 → 어제 산 제 가방 (my bag that I bought yesterday).

English puts "that" or "my" at the very start ("that person I met"), so learners often write 그 내가 만난 사람. That sounds wrong in Korean; keep 그 next to 사람.

examples.ko: 내가 어제 만난 그 사람은 정말 솔직했어.
examples.en: That person I met yesterday was really frank.

examples.ko: 우리가 매일 이용하는 이 버스는 항상 늦어요.
examples.en: This bus we use every day is always late.

examples.ko: 선생님이 읽은 저의 글은 환경에 대한 글이에요.
examples.en: My writing that the teacher read is about the environment.

examples.ko: 어제 산 제 가방이 너무 작아요.
examples.en: My bag that I bought yesterday is too small.

examples.ko: 제가 자주 가는 그 식당은 오늘 문을 안 열었어요.
examples.en: That restaurant I often go to didn't open today.
Who is that person over there that we saw earlier?

lessons.title: Lesson 29: Changing Verbs to Nouns with ~기 and 음/ㅁ

vocab.en: to search for, to surf the internet
to cross over, to climb over

grammar.explanation:
~기 turns a verb or adjective into a noun meaning "doing X" or "being X": 말하다 → 말하기 (speaking). The new noun takes particles like any other, so 말하기가 어려워요 is "speaking is difficult".

Just add ~기 to the stem, whatever its last letter: 쓰다 → 쓰 + 기 → 쓰기, 먹다 → 먹기, 살다 → 살기. Irregulars don't change, because ~기 starts with a consonant: 듣다 → 듣기, 돕다 → 돕기.

~기 is most common before words that judge how easy or pleasant something is: 쉽다, 어렵다, 좋다, 편하다, 불편하다. The particle 가 is often dropped there: 살기 좋아요 (good to live in).

How is it different from ~는 것? Both mean "doing X", and often either works. ~기 fits best in these set patterns and in lists; with 좋아하다 and 싫어하다, ~는 것 is more common (요리하는 것을 좋아해요).

examples.en: Speaking in Korean is difficult.
This dictionary is convenient to use.
This village is a nice place to live.
Korean songs are nice to listen to.
examples.note: Irregular stems don't change before ~기: 듣다 → 듣기.

examples.en: This chair is uncomfortable to sit on.
Writing Korean is easier than speaking it.

grammar.explanation:
~기 시작하다 means "to start doing X". ~기 names the action as a noun, and 시작하다 says it began: 비가 오기 시작했어요 is "it started to rain".

Form it as stem + 기 + 시작하다: 오다 → 오기 시작하다, 먹다 → 먹기 시작하다, 만들다 → 만들기 시작하다. The first verb never changes for tense. All the tense goes on 시작하다: 시작해요 (start), 시작했어요 (started), 시작할 거예요 (will start).

A common mistake is putting the past on the first verb (왔기 시작했어요). Keep it as a plain stem + 기. You can also start the action from an adjective that has become a verb with ~아/어지다: 추워지다 → 추워지기 시작했어요 (it started getting cold).

examples.en: It suddenly started to rain.
I started studying Korean last year.
People started to gather in the village.
I'm going to start exercising next month.
The baby started walking.
examples.note: 걷다 doesn't change before ~기: 걷 + 기 → 걷기.

examples.en: The weather has started getting cold these days.

grammar.explanation:
~기 싫다 means "I don't want to do X". It is the opposite of ~고 싶다: 일하고 싶어요 (I want to work) vs 일하기 싫어요 (I don't want to work). It is stronger than 일하고 싶지 않아요, closer to "I hate to".

Form it as stem + 기 + 싫다: 일하다 → 일하기 싫어요, 먹다 → 먹기 싫어요, 일어나다 → 일어나기 싫어요. For the past, change only 싫다: 가기 싫었어요 (I didn't want to go).

싫다 is an adjective that describes your own feelings, so use it for "I" in statements and for "you" in questions. For anyone else, use the verb 싫어하다: 동생은 청소하기 싫어해요. This is the same 싫다 / 싫어하다 split you saw in Lesson 8.

examples.en: I don't want to work today.
I don't want to get up early in the morning.
My younger sibling hates cleaning the room.
I don't want to do anything today.
Yesterday I didn't want to go to school.
Why don't you want to go to the hospital?

grammar.explanation:
Because ~기 makes a short noun out of a verb, Korean uses it where English uses a bare command or label: buttons, menus, signs, instructions and to-do lists. 보다 → 보기 (View), 열다 → 열기 (Open), 닫다 → 닫기 (Close), 찾다 → 찾기 (Find), 검색하다 → 검색하기 (Search).

The stem never changes, so this is an easy place to practise ~기. Phone screens are full of these: 사진 보기, 다시 하기. In a to-do list, write one item per line or join them with 와/과: 숙제하기와 운동하기.

Read these as labels, not full sentences. To actually tell someone to do it, you still need a sentence ending: 열기를 누르세요 (press Open), or 문을 열어 주세요 (please open the door).

examples.ko: 오늘 할 일은 쌀 사기와 방 청소하기예요.
examples.en: Today's to-dos are buying rice and cleaning my room.

examples.ko: 사진을 크게 보고 싶으면 확대하기 버튼을 누르세요.
examples.en: If you want to see the photo bigger, press the zoom button.
If you want to open the file, press Open.

examples.ko: 이번 주 목표는 매일 한국어 듣기예요.
examples.en: This week's goal is listening to Korean every day.
The Search button is at the top of the screen.
After you finish reading, press Close.

grammar.explanation:
~ㅁ/음 is another way to turn a verb or adjective into a noun. Today you mostly meet it in everyday nouns that came from verbs, and in short written statements such as notices and memos.

After a vowel, put ㅁ under the last syllable: 기쁘다 → 기쁘 + ㅁ → 기쁨 (joy), 싸우다 → 싸움 (fight), 꾸다 → 꿈 (dream). After a consonant, add 음: 웃다 → 웃 + 음 → 웃음 (laughter), 죽다 → 죽음 (death). ㄹ-stems keep the ㄹ and add ㅁ under it: 살다 → 삶 (life). Irregulars change as they do before a vowel: 돕다 → 도움 (help), 걷다 → 걸음 (step).

As a beginner, learn the common ones as vocabulary (도움, 기쁨, 싸움, 느낌, 웃음, 꿈) rather than making new ones. To turn an action into a noun in your own sentences, ~는 것 and ~기 are much more common.

examples.en: I need my friend's help.

examples.ko: 그 소식을 듣고 큰 기쁨을 느꼈어요.
examples.en: I felt great joy when I heard that news.
I had a fight with my younger sibling yesterday.
I have a strange feeling.
That person laughs a lot.
I had a strange dream last night.
What is life in Korea like?
examples.note: 살다 keeps its ㄹ: 살 + ㅁ → 삶.

lessons.title: Lesson 30: An uncertain clause with ~는지, I have been doing X for…: ~ㄴ/은 지 X 됐다

vocab.en: to take out, to remove something
to raise (a child, pet), to cultivate (a plant)
to break up with a person
to be reduced, to be decreased

grammar.explanation:
~는지 turns a question into one part of a bigger sentence. "When is the delivery coming?" becomes "I don't know when the delivery is coming". It usually comes before verbs of knowing and asking: 알다, 모르다, 궁금하다, 물어보다. The clause often has a question word (언제, 어디, 왜, 뭐, 누가); without one it means "whether".

For verbs in the present, add ~는지 to the stem: 오다 → 오는지, 먹다 → 먹는지. ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ: 살다 → 사는지, 열다 → 여는지. 있다 and 없다 also take ~는지: 있는지, 없는지. For the past, add ~는지 after ~았/었: 갔는지, 먹었는지. For the future or a guess, use ~ㄹ/을지: 올지, 먹을지.

The question word stays in its normal place inside the clause: 어디에 사는지 (where (he) lives). The end of the whole sentence decides whether it is a statement (몰라요) or a question (알아요?).

examples.en: I don't know when the delivery is coming.
Do you know where that person lives?
I asked my friend why he got angry.
I'm not sure if it will rain tomorrow.

examples.ko: 이 식당이 몇 시에 문을 여는지 알아요?
examples.en: Do you know what time this restaurant opens?
examples.note: 열다 is an ㄹ-stem: 열 + 는지 → 여는지.

examples.en: I'm curious who came yesterday.
I still haven't been able to decide what to eat.

grammar.explanation:
In the present, adjectives take ~ㄴ/은지 instead of ~는지, just as they use ~ㄴ/은 to describe nouns. After a vowel add ~ㄴ지: 비싸다 → 비싼지, 크다 → 큰지. After a consonant add ~은지: 많다 → 많은지, 좋다 → 좋은지. Irregulars apply as usual: 춥다 → 추운지, 가깝다 → 가까운지, 멀다 → 먼지 (ㄹ drops).

이다 always becomes ~인지: 얼마이다 → 얼마인지, 학생이다 → 학생인지.

Only the present is different. In the past, adjectives use ~았/었는지 like verbs (추웠는지, 비쌌는지), and the guess or future form is ~ㄹ/을지 (추울지). A common mistake is 비싸는지: adjectives never take ~는 in the present. The exception is 있다/없다 words, which take ~는지 (재미있는지, 맛없는지).

examples.en: Do you know how cold it is outside?
I'll ask which exit is closer.
I don't know how much the subway fare is.
Do you know how far it is from home to school?
examples.note: 멀다 drops ㄹ: 멀 + ㄴ지 → 먼지.

examples.en: I asked whether that restaurant's food is good.
examples.note: 있다 words take ~는지, not ~은지.

examples.en: I asked my friend whether yesterday's exam was hard.

grammar.explanation:
To say "whether or not", write the clause twice: first the positive, then 안 + the same verb with the same ending. 오다 → 오는지 안 오는지 (whether (he) comes or not). Then finish with 알다, 모르다, 물어보다 or 궁금하다.

Use the right ending for each kind of word. Verbs: 먹는지 안 먹는지. Adjectives: 싼지 안 싼지, 좋은지 안 좋은지. Past: 왔는지 안 왔는지. For 하다-verbs, 안 goes right before 하다 and the noun part isn't repeated: 공부하는지 안 하는지.

Some words have their own opposite, so you use that instead of 안. For 이다, use 아닌지: 학생인지 아닌지. For 있다, use 없는지: 있는지 없는지.

examples.en: I don't know whether he is coming or not.

examples.ko: 이 가격이 싼지 안 싼지 모르겠어요.
examples.en: I can't tell whether this price is cheap or not.

examples.ko: 수술이 잘 됐는지 안 됐는지 아직 몰라요.
examples.en: We don't know yet whether the surgery went well or not.

examples.ko: 동생이 숙제를 했는지 안 했는지 몰라요.
examples.en: I don't know whether my younger sibling did the homework or not.
I don't know whether that person is a student or not.
Do you know whether there's milk in the fridge or not?

grammar.explanation:
~ㄹ/을지도 모르다 says something "might" happen or "might" be true. It comes from ~ㄹ/을지 + 도 + 모르다; the 도 adds little meaning, so learn it as one set phrase. It is almost always used as 몰라요.

Add ~ㄹ지도 after a vowel and ~을지도 after a consonant: 오다 → 올지도 몰라요, 작다 → 작을지도 몰라요, 위험하다 → 위험할지도 몰라요. ㄹ-stems just add 지도: 멀다 → 멀지도 몰라요. Irregulars change before 을: 춥다 → 추울지도, 듣다 → 들을지도. For something that might already have happened, use the past: 갔을지도 몰라요 (may have gone).

Don't confuse it with ~ㄹ/을지 모르겠어요 ("I'm not sure whether..."). That one focuses on not knowing; ~ㄹ/을지도 몰라요 focuses on the possibility.

examples.en: It might rain tomorrow.
That person may have already left.
These stairs might be dangerous.
The roads might be jammed today.
These clothes might be small for me.
Tomorrow might be colder than today.
examples.note: 춥다: ㅂ becomes 우 before 을, so 추울지도.

grammar.point: ~ㄴ/은 지 (time) 되다 (it has been X since)
grammar.explanation:
This pattern says how much time has passed since something happened. 한국에 온 지 일 년 됐어요 is literally "since coming to Korea, it has become a year". English says "It's been a year since I came to Korea", or often "I've been in Korea for a year".

Build it in three parts: past modifier + 지, then the length of time, then 되다 (almost always 됐어요). After a vowel use ~ㄴ 지: 오다 → 온 지, 시작하다 → 시작한 지. After a consonant use ~은 지: 먹다 → 먹은 지. ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ: 살다 → 산 지. Irregulars as usual: 듣다 → 들은 지.

Watch the spacing: here 지 means "time since", so there is a space before it (온 지), unlike the ~는지 question ending (오는지). Ask "how long has it been?" with 얼마나 됐어요?. You can also use 지나다 instead of 되다: 일 년이 지났어요 (a year has passed).

examples.ko: 한국에 온 지 일 년 됐어요.
examples.en: It has been a year since I came to Korea.

examples.ko: 그 사람과 헤어진 지 한 달 됐어요.
examples.en: It has been a month since I broke up with that person.
How long has it been since you started your part-time job?

examples.ko: 밥을 먹은 지 세 시간 됐어요.
examples.en: It has been three hours since I ate.

examples.ko: 서울에 산 지 오 년 됐어요.
examples.en: I've been living in Seoul for five years.
examples.note: 살다 drops ㄹ: 산 지.

examples.ko: 이 회사에서 일한 지 벌써 십 년이 지났어요.
examples.en: Ten years have already passed since I started working at this company.
It's been a long time since I met my friend.

vocab.en: to raise (children), to train (animals), to develop (skills)

grammar.point: Describing nouns with 이다: N1인 N2
grammar.explanation:
이다 ("to be") behaves like an adjective, so to describe a noun it takes the adjective modifier ~ㄴ. Noun + 이다 becomes noun + 인: 부자이다 → 부자인. Then put the second noun after it: 부자인 친구 is "a friend who is rich".

It is always 인, whether the first noun ends in a vowel or a consonant: 의사 → 의사인, 학생 → 학생인. This is different from the polite ending, where 이에요 and 예요 change with the noun.

Use it when the first noun tells you something about the second: a job (간호사인 언니, my older sister who is a nurse), a status (동갑인 친구) or a quality (불법인 일). For the past, use 이었던 after a consonant and 였던 after a vowel: 선생님이었던 아버지, 가수였던 친구.

examples.en: My friend who is rich paid for the meal.

examples.ko: 선생님인 우리 언니는 매일 일찍 일어나요.
examples.en: My older sister, who is a teacher, gets up early every day.
I have a lot of friends who are the same age as me.
You must not do things that are illegal.
My younger sibling, who is a university student, lives in Seoul.

examples.ko: 가수인 친구가 다음 달에 공연을 해요.
examples.en: My friend who is a singer is giving a performance next month.

examples.ko: 선생님이었던 우리 아버지는 지금 농장에서 일해요.
examples.en: My father, who used to be a teacher, now works on a farm.
examples.note: Past of 인: 이었던 after a consonant, 였던 after a vowel.

grammar.explanation:
~인지 is the ~는지 pattern from Lesson 30 applied to 이다. Since 이다 is adjective-like, it takes ~ㄴ지, giving 인지: 누구이다 → 누구인지, 얼마이다 → 얼마인지, 학생이다 → 학생인지. Use it to fold a "who / what / where / how much is it?" question into a bigger sentence with 알다, 모르다, 물어보다 or 궁금하다.

To build one, start from the direct question and swap the ending: 이 반지가 얼마예요? → 이 반지가 얼마인지 + 알아요? After a vowel, speech often shortens 인지 to ㄴ지: 누구인지 → 누군지, 어디인지 → 어딘지, 뭐인지 → 뭔지.

For the past, use 이었는지 / 였는지: 누구였는지 (who it was). For "whether or not", add 아닌지: 진짜인지 아닌지 (whether it's real or not).

examples.en: Do you know how much this ring is?
I don't know who that person is.
I asked where city hall is.
Do you know what this means?
I forgot what day of the week it is today.

examples.ko: 어제 전화한 사람이 누구였는지 기억이 안 나요.
examples.en: I can't remember who the person who called yesterday was.
examples.note: Past of 인지: 였는지 after a vowel, 이었는지 after a consonant.

grammar.point: ~인 것 (the fact that X is Y)
grammar.explanation:
Add 것 after N인 and a whole "X is Y" statement becomes a noun: 그 사람이 의사이다 (that person is a doctor) → 그 사람이 의사인 것 (the fact that that person is a doctor). This is the 이다 version of ~는 것, and you use it the same way, as a subject or object.

Step by step: 오늘이 생일이에요 → 오늘이 생일인 것 → 오늘이 생일인 것을 몰랐어요 (I didn't know that today is (your) birthday). It is common with 알다, 모르다, 잊어버리다, 깨닫다 and with feeling words like 신기하다 or 놀랍다. In speech, 것을 shrinks to 걸 and 것이 to 게.

For something that used to be true, use 이었던 것 / 였던 것: 그 사람이 가수였던 것 (the fact that that person used to be a singer).

examples.en: I didn't know that person was a doctor.

examples.ko: 오늘이 친구 생일인 것을 아까 깨달았어요.
examples.en: I realized earlier that today is my friend's birthday.
It's amazing that we are the same age.
I forgot that today is Sunday.
examples.note: 걸 is the spoken short form of 것을.

examples.ko: 이 식당 음식이 무료인 것이 놀라웠어요.
examples.en: It was surprising that the food at this restaurant is free.
Did you know that person used to be a singer?

vocab.en: some sort of hard time or hardship
to put on shoes or socks
to put shoes or socks on somebody
to cut off, to quit something
to search for a worker, to search for a job, to get a job

grammar.explanation:
~(으)려고 links two actions: the first is your goal, the second is what you do to reach it. 한국어를 배우려고 한국에 왔어요 is "I came to Korea (in order) to learn Korean".

After a vowel or ㄹ, add ~려고: 가다 → 가려고, 배우다 → 배우려고, 만들다 → 만들려고 (the ㄹ stays). After any other consonant, add ~으려고: 먹다 → 먹으려고, 찍다 → 찍으려고. Irregulars change before 으: 듣다 → 들으려고, 돕다 → 도우려고.

The tense goes only on the final verb, never on the ~(으)려고 verb: 사려고 갔어요, not 샀으려고. Both halves normally have the same subject. Also, you can't end the sentence with a request like ~세요 after ~(으)려고; ~(으)러 (later this lesson) can do that.

examples.en: I'm saving money to go on a trip.
I came to Korea to learn Korean.
I bought tickets in advance to see the performance.
I wrote a resume to find a job.
I bought eggs to make a cake.
examples.note: 만들다 keeps its ㄹ and adds 려고, with no 으.

examples.en: I took out my earphones to listen to music.
examples.note: 듣다: ㄷ becomes ㄹ before 으, so 들으려고.

examples.en: I brought a camera to take photos.

grammar.explanation:
Put 하다 after ~(으)려고 and it becomes a sentence ending meaning "plan to" or "intend to": 연락하려고 해요 is "I'm planning to contact (them)". It is less certain than ~ㄹ/을 거예요, more like "I'm thinking of doing it".

Form it the same way as ~(으)려고: 가다 → 가려고 해요, 먹다 → 먹으려고 해요, 만들다 → 만들려고 해요. In the past, 가려고 했어요 means "I was going to go", and it often hints that it didn't happen.

Swap 하다 for 노력하다 (to make an effort) and it means "try hard to": 끊으려고 노력하고 있어요 (I'm trying hard to quit). Don't confuse this with ~아/어 보다 (later this lesson), which means "try it and see", not "make an effort".

examples.en: I'm trying hard to quit smoking.
I plan to contact my friend tomorrow.
We tried hard to solve that problem.
I'm planning to rest at home this weekend.
I was going to go to bed early yesterday.
examples.note: The past 했어요 often hints the plan didn't work out.

examples.en: I try hard to speak in Korean every day.

grammar.explanation:
~(으)러 says why you are going or coming somewhere: 놀러 왔어요 is "(I) came to hang out". It must be followed by a movement verb such as 가다, 오다, 나가다 or 다니다.

After a vowel or ㄹ, add ~러: 보다 → 보러, 놀다 → 놀러 (the ㄹ stays). After another consonant, add ~으러: 먹다 → 먹으러, 찾다 → 찾으러. Irregulars change before 으: 듣다 → 들으러, 걷다 → 걸으러. The tense goes on the movement verb: 먹으러 갔어요.

How it differs from ~(으)려고: ~(으)러 only works with movement verbs, while ~(으)려고 works with any verb (돈을 모으려고 일해요, but not 모으러 일해요). On the other hand, ~(으)러 can be used in requests and suggestions (같이 먹으러 가요!), which ~(으)려고 can't.

examples.en: I went to the dentist to get a tooth pulled.
My friend came over to my house to hang out.
I went to the changing room to change clothes.
Do you want to go out to eat lunch?

examples.ko: 주말에 친구와 영화를 보러 갈 거예요.
examples.en: This weekend I'm going to go see a movie with a friend.
I came to the library to find a book.
Let's go get coffee together.
examples.note: ~(으)러 works in suggestions; ~(으)려고 doesn't.

grammar.explanation:
~아/어 보다 means "try doing" in the sense of "do it and see what it's like", not "make an effort". 먹어 보세요 is "try eating it", and 신어 봐도 돼요? is "can I try them on?".

First make the ~아/어 form of the verb (the 요 form without 요), then add 보다. Stems with ㅏ or ㅗ take 아: 가다 → 가 보다, 오다 → 와 보다. Others take 어: 먹다 → 먹어 보다, 마시다 → 마셔 보다. 하다 → 해 보다. Irregulars change as usual: 듣다 → 들어 보다. Then conjugate 보다: 봐요, 봤어요, 보세요, 볼 거예요.

In the past, ~아/어 봤어요 means you have tried or experienced something: 한국 음식을 먹어 봤어요 (I've tried Korean food), 가 봤어요 (I've been there). To negate it, put 안 before the whole thing: 안 먹어 봤어요. For "try hard to", use ~(으)려고 노력하다 instead.

examples.en: Try this kimchi.
May I try on these shoes?

examples.ko: 어제 처음으로 한국 음식을 만들어 봤어요.
examples.en: Yesterday I tried making Korean food for the first time.
Give this song a listen.
examples.note: 듣다 → 들어, then add 보세요.

examples.en: Have you been to Busan?
I haven't tried making kimchi yet.

grammar.explanation:
적 is a noun meaning "a time (in your past)". Describe it with the past modifier and add 있다 or 없다: ~ㄴ/은 적이 있다 means "have done before", ~ㄴ/은 적이 없다 means "have never done".

After a vowel, use ~ㄴ 적: 만나다 → 만난 적, 하다 → 한 적. After a consonant, use ~은 적: 먹다 → 먹은 적, 읽다 → 읽은 적. ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ: 살다 → 산 적. Irregulars as usual: 듣다 → 들은 적, 돕다 → 도운 적.

It is very often combined with ~아/어 보다, which adds the sense of trying or experiencing: 가 본 적이 있어요 (I've been there), 먹어 본 적이 없어요 (I've never tried it). It talks about experience at some point in life, so don't use it for something you did just now or do regularly. For "I ate this morning", just say 아침을 먹었어요.

examples.en: I have met a celebrity before.
Have you ever been to Korea?
I have never been drunk.
I have never seen a miracle like that.
Have you ever lived in Korea?
examples.note: 살다 drops ㄹ: 산 적.

examples.en: I've never heard that song.
examples.note: 듣다: ㄷ becomes ㄹ before 은, so 들은.

examples.en: I've never tried traveling alone.

vocab.en: a kind of group blind date
a building with a bunch of stores in it
to raise, to lift, to increase
to be hurt, to be damaged
to be right, to be proper, to be correct

grammar.explanation:
중 means "middle", so verb stem + ~는 중이다 means "to be in the middle of doing". 밥을 먹는 중이에요 is "I'm (in the middle of) eating". It is often used to explain why you can't do something right now: "I'm on my way", "I'm working on it".

Form it like ~는 것, with 중 in place of 것: 먹다 → 먹는 중, 가다 → 가는 중, 만들다 → 만드는 중 (ㄹ drops). Then add 이다: 중이에요 (am doing), 중이었어요 (was doing). Use it only with verbs, not adjectives.

The meaning is close to ~고 있다 (먹고 있어요), and often both work. ~는 중이다 stresses that the action has started and isn't finished yet. ~고 있다 is more flexible: it also covers long-term situations (서울에 살고 있어요), where ~는 중이다 can sound odd.

examples.en: I'm eating right now.
We are in the middle of filming a new movie.
I was in the middle of writing a letter to my friend.
I'm on my way home now.
My younger sibling is in the middle of making a cake.
examples.note: 만들다 drops ㄹ before 는: 만드는 중.

examples.en: What are you doing right now?

grammar.explanation:
With nouns that make 하다-verbs (공사하다, 수업하다, 회의하다, 통화하다, 운전하다), you can put 중 right after the noun and skip ~하는: 회의하는 중 → 회의 중. It means the same thing, "in the middle of a meeting", only shorter.

This short form is everywhere on signs and screens: 공사 중 (under construction), 회의 중 (in a meeting), 영업 중 (open for business), 통화 중 (on the phone). In a sentence, add 이다 or 에: 지금 회의 중이에요 (I'm in a meeting now), 수업 중에 (during class). Add 는 for contrast or emphasis: 강의 중에는 (during the lecture, at least).

It only works with 하다-nouns. 먹다 has no noun part, so it must be 먹는 중.

examples.en: This building is under construction now.
The teacher is in a consultation right now.
Please turn off your cell phone during the lecture.
I'm on the phone right now.
I got a phone call while driving.
Is that restaurant open right now?

grammar.explanation:
동안 is a noun meaning "period of time". You've used it after time words (세 시간 동안, for three hours). After a verb + ~는, it means "during the time that", or "while": 요리하는 동안 is "while (I) cook".

Form it as stem + ~는 + 동안: 자다 → 자는 동안, 기다리다 → 기다리는 동안, 먹다 → 먹는 동안, 살다 → 사는 동안 (ㄹ drops). 있다 works too: 있는 동안. The verb before 동안 stays in the ~는 form even when the story is in the past; the tense goes on the last verb. Write 자는 동안 비가 왔어요 (it rained while I slept), not 잤는 동안.

The two halves can have different subjects (제가 요리하는 동안 동생은...). Use it with actions that last a while, like sleeping, waiting or living somewhere, not with instant ones like arriving.

examples.ko: 제가 요리하는 동안 동생은 텔레비전을 봤어요.
examples.en: While I cooked, my younger sibling watched TV.

examples.ko: 한국에 사는 동안 친구를 많이 사귀었어요.
examples.en: I made a lot of friends while living in Korea.
I read a book while waiting for my friend.
Did someone call while I was sleeping?

examples.ko: 밥을 먹는 동안 휴대폰을 보지 않아요.
examples.en: I don't look at my phone while I eat.

examples.ko: 부산에 있는 동안 바다를 매일 봤어요.
examples.en: I saw the sea every day while I was in Busan.

grammar.explanation:
중에 after a group of nouns means "among" or "(out of) between". You can list the choices with 와/과, 하고 or (이)랑 (사과와 딸기 중에), or use a plural or group word (친구들 중에, 우리 가족 중에). It is usually followed by a superlative with 제일 / 가장, or a question like 뭐가 더 ...?

Step by step: list the options, add 중에, then say which one: 커피하고 차 중에 + 뭐가 더 좋아요? 중에서 means the same as 중에, and 이 중에 / 이 중에서 means "out of these". The vocab word 그중 ("among them") is the same idea.

The group can be a whole described noun: 제가 본 영화 + 중에 → 제가 본 영화 중에 (of the movies I've seen).

examples.ko: 사과와 딸기 중에 뭐가 더 좋아요?
examples.en: Between apples and strawberries, which do you like more?

examples.ko: 제 친구들 중에 민수가 키가 제일 커요.
examples.en: Among my friends, Minsu is the tallest.

examples.ko: 제가 본 영화 중에 이 영화가 제일 재미있었어요.
examples.en: Of all the movies I have seen, this one was the most fun.

examples.ko: 이 중에서 어느 게 제일 싸요?
examples.en: Which of these is the cheapest?
examples.note: 중에서 means the same as 중에.

examples.ko: 우리 가족 중에 제가 제일 키가 작아요.
examples.en: I'm the shortest in my family.

examples.ko: 제가 가 본 나라 중에 일본이 제일 가까워요.
examples.en: Of the countries I've been to, Japan is the closest.

grammar.explanation:
Time word + 중으로 means "at some point within that time". You plan or promise to get something done before that period ends, without naming the exact moment: 이번 주 중으로 끝낼게요 is "I'll finish it sometime this week". It sounds a little formal and is common at work.

Just put 중으로 after the time noun: 오늘 → 오늘 중으로, 내일 → 내일 중으로, 이번 달 → 이번 달 중으로, 올해 → 올해 중으로. The sentence usually ends in the future (~ㄹ/을 거예요, ~ㄹ게요) or a request (~주세요), because it is about a deadline.

Compare it with 까지 (by / until a point): 금요일까지 is "by Friday", a fixed deadline, while 이번 주 중으로 is a looser "sometime this week". It also differs from 안에 / 이내에 (Lesson 24), which count a length of time (삼 일 안에, within three days) rather than naming a period on the calendar.

examples.en: I'll finish the work sometime this week.

examples.ko: 다음 달 중으로 계약을 할 거예요.
examples.en: We will sign the contract sometime next month.
Please contact me sometime today.
The package will arrive sometime tomorrow.
I'm going to learn to drive sometime this year.

examples.ko: 이번 달 중으로 돈을 보내 주세요.
examples.en: Please send the money sometime this month.
